questions.question: How do you define optimal solution? Does greedy algorithm always guarantee optimal solution? Given the string 'SUPER DUPER CSIT', use a Greedy algorithm to build a Huffman tree.
questions.answer: An optimal solution is one that achieves the best possible value of the objective function (maximum or minimum) among all feasible solutions. Greedy algorithms do not always guarantee an optimal solution — they make locally optimal choices at each step, which may not lead to a globally optimal solution. However, for specific problems like Huffman coding and Fractional Knapsack, greedy does give an optimal solution. For Huffman coding on 'SUPER DUPER CSIT': first count character frequencies (S:3, U:2, P:2, E:2, R:2, D:1, C:1, I:1, T:1, space:1), then repeatedly merge the two lowest-frequency nodes into a subtree, building the Huffman tree bottom-up. Assign 0/1 to left/right branches to get prefix codes. Higher frequency characters receive shorter codes.

questions.question: What is order statistics? Write and analyze the algorithm for randomized quick sort.
questions.answer: Order statistics refer to finding the i-th smallest (or largest) element in a set. The i-th order statistic is the i-th smallest element. Randomized Quick Sort modifies Quick Sort by randomly selecting a pivot before partitioning. Algorithm: RANDOMIZED-QUICKSORT(A, p, r): if p < r, q = RANDOMIZED-PARTITION(A, p, r), then recurse on A[p..q-1] and A[q+1..r]. RANDOMIZED-PARTITION selects a random index i in [p,r], swaps A[i] with A[r], then calls standard PARTITION. Analysis: Best and Average case O(n log n), Worst case O(n²) but randomization makes worst case extremely unlikely. Expected time is O(n log n).

questions.question: Distinguish between dynamic programming and memorization. Parenthesize the matrices A(30x1), B(1x40), C(40x10) and D(10x15) for computing matrix multiplication using dynamic programming.
questions.answer: Dynamic Programming solves subproblems bottom-up, storing results in a table. Memoization is top-down DP — it uses recursion but caches results of subproblems to avoid recomputation. DP fills the table iteratively; memoization fills it on demand. For matrix chain multiplication of A(30x1), B(1x40), C(40x10), D(10x15): dimensions p = [30,1,40,10,15]. Compute m[i][j] table: m[1][2]=30x1x40=1200, m[2][3]=1x40x10=400, m[3][4]=40x10x15=6000, m[1][3]=min(m[1][2]+m[2][3]+30x40x10, m[1][1]+m[2][3]+30x1x10)=min(13600,700)=700, m[2][4]=min(m[2][2]+m[3][4]+1x40x15, m[2][3]+m[3][4]+1x10x15)=min(6600,550)=550, m[1][4]=min(m[1][1]+m[2][4]+30x1x15, m[1][2]+m[3][4]+30x40x15, m[1][3]+m[3][4]+30x10x15)=min(1000,24200,10200)=1000. Optimal parenthesization: ((A)(BCD)) or equivalently (A((BC)D)) with cost 1000.

questions.question: Solve the recurrence relation T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n using recursion tree method.
questions.answer: Draw the recursion tree. At level 0: cost n. At level 1: two subproblems each of size n/2, cost n/2 each → total n. At level 2: four subproblems each of size n/4, cost n/4 each → total n. Pattern: each level costs n. Tree height = log₂n (since we divide by 2 each time). Number of levels = log₂n + 1. Total cost = n × (log₂n + 1) = O(n log n). Therefore T(n) = Θ(n log n).

questions.question: Find the best and worst case for Bubble sort.
questions.answer: Bubble Sort repeatedly swaps adjacent elements if they are in the wrong order. Best Case: Array is already sorted. With optimization (flag to detect no swaps), only one pass is needed. Time: O(n). Space: O(1). Worst Case: Array is sorted in reverse order. Every pair of adjacent elements must be swapped. Number of comparisons = n(n-1)/2. Time: O(n²). Space: O(1).

questions.question: Using Extended Euclidean Algorithm, find the GCD of 12 and 16.
questions.answer: Extended Euclidean Algorithm finds GCD(a,b) and coefficients x, y such that ax + by = gcd(a,b). GCD(12,16): 16 = 1×12 + 4; 12 = 3×4 + 0. GCD = 4. Back-substitution: 4 = 16 - 1×12. So x = -1, y = 1: 12×(-1) + 16×1 = 4. GCD(12,16) = 4.

questions.question: Find all possible subsets of the integers that sum to 21 in the array {5, 6, 10, 11, 15} using backtracking technique.
questions.answer: Using backtracking, generate all subsets and check if their sum equals 21. Sort: {5,6,10,11,15}. Explore systematically with pruning when partial sum exceeds 21. Valid subsets: {5,6,10} (sum=21), {6,15} (sum=21), {10,11} (sum=21). These are all possible subsets that sum to 21.

questions.question: Define class P and NP problem. Why do we need approximation algorithms? Justify.
questions.answer: Class P: Problems solvable by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time. Examples: sorting, shortest path. Class NP: Problems whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time by a deterministic algorithm. All P problems are in NP. NP-Complete problems are the hardest in NP; no polynomial-time algorithm is known for them. Approximation Algorithms are needed because NP-complete problems (like TSP, Vertex Cover) have no known efficient exact solution. Rather than spending exponential time for exact answers, approximation algorithms find near-optimal solutions in polynomial time with a guaranteed approximation ratio.

questions.question: State the time and space complexity for sequential search. Write the rules for master theorem for finding asymptotic bounds.
questions.answer: Sequential Search: Best case O(1) (element at first position), Worst case O(n) (element at last or not found), Average case O(n). Space complexity O(1). Master Theorem: For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) where a≥1, b>1: Case 1: if f(n) = O(n^(log_b(a) - ε)) for ε>0, then T(n) = Θ(n^log_b(a)). Case 2: if f(n) = Θ(n^log_b(a)), then T(n) = Θ(n^log_b(a) × log n). Case 3: if f(n) = Ω(n^(log_b(a) + ε)) for ε>0 and regularity condition holds, then T(n) = Θ(f(n)).

questions.question: Justify the worst case for binary search. Find the edit distance from the string 'RELEVANT' to 'ELEPHANT' using dynamic programming approach.
questions.answer: Binary Search worst case is O(log n) — occurs when the element is not found or is at the last comparison point. Each step halves the search space, giving log₂n levels. Edit Distance between 'RELEVANT' and 'ELEPHANT': Using DP table where dp[i][j] = edit distance between first i chars of RELEVANT and first j chars of ELEPHANT. Fill table using: if chars match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; else dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]). Final edit distance = 3 (optimal operations: substitute R→E, delete E, insert P, or similar optimal path yielding 3).

questions.question: Distinguish between recursion and backtracking. Using Miller-Rabin primality test, check whether 53 is prime or not?
questions.answer: Recursion: A function calls itself to solve smaller subproblems. It always proceeds forward and trusts subproblem solutions. Backtracking: Tries all possibilities and undoes (backtracks) choices that don't lead to a valid solution. It is used for constraint satisfaction problems. Miller-Rabin test for 53: Write 53-1 = 52 = 4 × 13, so s=2, d=13. Choose a=2: compute 2^13 mod 53 = 30. Since 30 ≠ 1 and ≠ 52, square: 30² mod 53 = 900 mod 53 = 52 ≡ -1. Since we got -1 before the last squaring, 53 passes for a=2. Conclusion: 53 is prime.

questions.question: How does 0/1 Knapsack problem differ from fractional one? Find the minimum vertex cover in the given graph.
questions.answer: 0/1 Knapsack: Items cannot be broken — either take the whole item (1) or leave it (0). Solved by DP in O(nW). Fractional Knapsack: Items can be broken into fractions. Solved greedily by sorting by value/weight ratio in O(n log n). For minimum vertex cover in the given graph (11 vertices A-K): Apply the 2-approximation algorithm — find a maximal matching and take both endpoints. One valid maximal matching: {(A,J),(B,I),(C,D),(E,K),(F,G)}. Vertex cover = {A,J,B,I,C,D,E,K,F,G} plus H (to cover edge G-H or H-C). Size ≈ 10. Exact minimum is hard (NP-Complete), but approximation guarantees cover ≤ 2×OPT.

questions.question: Differentiate between dynamic programming and memorization. Compute the shortest path between every pair in the following graph using Floyd-Warshall algorithm. [Graph: Directed weighted graph with vertices A, B, C and edges A→B(4), B→A(1), B→C(2), A→C(7), C→A(6)]
questions.answer: Dynamic Programming: Bottom-up approach, fills table iteratively, no recursive overhead, always computes all subproblems. Memoization: Top-down approach, uses recursion with caching, computes only needed subproblems, has recursive call overhead. Floyd-Warshall on the given graph: Initial D⁰ = [[0,4,7],[1,0,2],[6,∞,0]]. After k=A: D¹ = [[0,4,7],[1,0,2],[6,10,0]]. After k=B: D² = [[0,4,6],[1,0,2],[6,10,0]] (A→C via B = 4+2=6 < 7). After k=C: D³ = [[0,4,6],[1,0,2],[6,10,0]] (no change). Final all-pairs shortest paths: A→B=4, A→C=6, B→A=1, B→C=2, C→A=6, C→B=10.

questions.question: What is the worst case of quick sort and how does randomized quick sort handle this problem? Sort the data {-2, 4, -3, 6, 12, 10, 11, 13, 9} using quick sort.
questions.answer: Quick Sort worst case O(n²) occurs when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element (already sorted or reverse sorted array). Randomized Quick Sort handles this by randomly selecting the pivot, making worst case extremely unlikely in practice and achieving expected O(n log n). Sorting {-2, 4, -3, 6, 12, 10, 11, 13, 9} with pivot = last element (9): partition around 9 → [-2, 4, -3, 6, 9, 12, 10, 11, 13]. Recurse on left {-2,4,-3,6} with pivot 6 → [-3, -2, 4, 6]. Recurse on right {12,10,11,13} with pivot 13 → [12, 10, 11, 13]. Continue: left of 6 → [-3, -2, 4]; right of 6 empty. For {12,10,11,13} pivot 11 → [10, 11, 12, 13]. Final sorted: [-3, -2, 4, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13].

questions.question: Does greedy algorithm guarantee optimal solution? Solve the Fractional knapsack problem to find maximum loot from given information. Items: 1-7, Values: 12,10,20,15,2,3,50, Weights: 2,1,3,2,12,10,1.
questions.answer: Greedy guarantees optimal solution for Fractional Knapsack but not for all problems. Calculate value/weight ratios: Item 7: 50/1=50, Item 2: 10/1=10, Item 4: 15/2=7.5, Item 3: 20/3=6.67, Item 1: 12/2=6, Item 6: 3/10=0.3, Item 5: 2/12=0.17. Sort descending by ratio. Assuming capacity W (not explicitly given in extracted text, typically 15-20 kg in such problems), greedily pick items by descending ratio, taking fractions if needed to fill capacity. For W=15: pick Item 7(1kg,50), Item 2(1kg,10), Item 4(2kg,15), Item 3(3kg,20), Item 1(2kg,12) = total weight 9kg, value 107. Continue with remaining capacity. [UNCERTAIN: exact knapsack capacity not specified in original paper extract; answer assumes standard capacity].

questions.question: Given a set A = {5, 7, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20}, find the subset that sums to 35 using backtracking.
Solve the following recurrence relations using master's method: (a) T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n³; (b) T(n) = 2T(n/4) + 1.
questions.answer: (a) T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n³: a=2, b=2, f(n)=n³. log_b(a) = log₂(2) = 1. f(n) = n³ = Ω(n^(1+ε)) for ε=2. Case 3 applies (check regularity: 2×(n/2)³ = n³/4 ≤ cn³ for c=1/4 < 1). T(n) = Θ(n³). (b) T(n) = 2T(n/4) + 1: a=2, b=4, f(n)=1. log_b(a) = log₄(2) = 0.5. f(n) = 1 = O(n^(0.5-ε)) for small ε. Case 1 applies. T(n) = Θ(n^0.5) = Θ(√n).

questions.question: Write an algorithm to find the nth Fibonacci number with its time and space complexity.
questions.answer: Iterative algorithm: FIB(n): if n≤1 return n; prev=0, curr=1; for i=2 to n: next=prev+curr; prev=curr; curr=next; return curr. Time complexity: O(n) — single loop runs n-1 times. Space complexity: O(1) — only three variables used. Recursive version has T(n)=T(n-1)+T(n-2) giving O(2ⁿ) time and O(n) stack space. DP version stores all values: O(n) time, O(n) space. The iterative approach is optimal for basic needs.

questions.question: Define order statistics problem. Find the edit distance between 'cat' and 'car' using dynamic programming.
questions.answer: Order Statistics: Finding the i-th smallest element in an unsorted array. The i-th order statistic is the element that would appear at position i in the sorted array. Edit Distance between 'cat' and 'car': Build DP table (4×4). Base: dp[i][0]=i, dp[0][j]=j. dp[1][1]: c==c → 0. dp[1][2]: c vs a → 1+min(0,1,1)=1. dp[1][3]: c vs r → 1+min(1,2,1)=2. dp[2][1]: a vs c → 1+min(1,0,1)=1. dp[2][2]: a==a → dp[1][1]=0. dp[2][3]: a vs r → 1+min(1,1,0)=1. dp[3][1]: t vs c → 2. dp[3][2]: t vs a → 2. dp[3][3]: t vs r → 1+min(2,2,1)=2. Wait, let me recompute carefully: cat vs car. c=c(0), c-a(1), c-r(2); a-c(1), a=a(0), a-r(1); t-c(2), t-a(2), t-r(1). Actually optimal: substitute t→r gives distance 1. dp[3][3] = 1 because t≠r, min(dp[2][3]=1, dp[3][2]=2, dp[2][2]=0) + 1 = 1. Edit distance = 1.

questions.question: Discuss about recursion and backtracking. Analyze the complexity of Miller-Rabin Randomized Primality test.
questions.answer: Recursion solves problems by breaking them into smaller identical subproblems and calling itself. Backtracking is a systematic trial-and-error approach that builds candidates incrementally and abandons a candidate ('backtracks') as soon as it determines the candidate cannot lead to a valid solution. Miller-Rabin Primality Test: For an odd integer n>2, write n-1=2ˢ × d. Choose k random witnesses a. For each: compute aᵈ mod n; if result is 1 or n-1, continue; else square s-1 times checking for n-1; if n-1 never appears, n is composite. Time complexity: O(k log³ n) or O(k log² n) per test using fast modular exponentiation. With k=log n witnesses, error probability ≤ (1/4)ᵏ = negligible.

questions.question: Solve the following linear equation using Chinese Remainder Theorem: x ≡ 1 (mod 3), x ≡ 2 (mod 5), x ≡ 0 (mod 7).
questions.answer: CRT: M = 3×5×7 = 105. M₁=35, M₂=21, M₃=15. Find inverses: 35 mod 3 = 2, inverse of 2 mod 3 = 2 (since 2×2=4≡1 mod 3). 21 mod 5 = 1, inverse = 1. 15 mod 7 = 1, inverse = 1. x = (1×35×2 + 2×21×1 + 0×15×1) mod 105 = (70 + 42 + 0) mod 105 = 112 mod 105 = 7. Verify: 7 mod 3 = 1 ✓, 7 mod 5 = 2 ✓, 7 mod 7 = 0 ✓. x = 7.

questions.question: Explain the approximation algorithm for vertex cover of a connected graph with an example.
questions.answer: Vertex Cover Approximation Algorithm: 1. Initialize C = empty set. 2. While there are uncovered edges: pick any edge (u,v); add both u and v to C; remove all edges incident to u or v. 3. Return C. This gives a 2-approximation: |C| ≤ 2×|OPT|. The edges chosen form a matching, and any vertex cover must include at least one endpoint of each matching edge. Since we include both, the ratio is at most 2. Example: Graph with edges {(A,B),(B,C),(C,D),(D,A),(A,C)}: Pick (A,B) → C={A,B}; remove edges incident to A,B; remaining: (C,D); pick (C,D) → C={A,B,C,D}. Size 4 ≤ 2×OPT (OPT=2 for this graph).

questions.question: State Cook's theorem. Discuss about problem reducibility.
questions.answer: Cook's Theorem (1971): SAT (Boolean satisfiability) is NP-Complete. It was the first problem proven to be NP-Complete, showing that every NP problem can be polynomially reduced to SAT. Reducibility: Problem A is polynomially reducible to problem B (A ≤ₚ B) if any instance of A can be transformed to an instance of B in polynomial time, such that the answer to A equals the answer to B. If B is easy, A is also easy. If A is hard, B is also hard. NP-Completeness proof: Show a problem is in NP (verify in polynomial time) and show some known NP-Complete problem reduces to it.

questions.question: Write short notes on: (a) Big Oh, Big Omega, Big Theta.
questions.answer: Big-O (O): Upper bound. f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist constants c>0 and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c×g(n) for all n≥n₀. Represents worst-case growth. Big-Ω (Omega): Lower bound. f(n) = Ω(g(n)) if there exist constants c>0 and n₀ such that f(n) ≥ c×g(n) for all n≥n₀. Represents best-case growth. Big-Θ (Theta): Tight bound. f(n) = Θ(g(n)) if f(n) = O(g(n)) and f(n) = Ω(g(n)). Both upper and lower bounds are the same asymptotically.

questions.question: Write short notes on: (b) Class P, Class NP and NP-Complete.
questions.answer: Class P: Decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time O(nᵏ). Examples: sorting, searching, shortest path. Class NP: Decision problems where a proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine. P ⊆ NP; whether P = NP is the greatest open problem in CS. NP-Complete: The hardest problems in NP. A problem X is NP-Complete if: (1) X ∈ NP, and (2) every problem in NP is polynomially reducible to X. Examples: SAT, Vertex Cover, Subset Sum, Hamiltonian Cycle.

questions.question: What is recurrence relation? How can it be solved? Show that time complexity of the recurrence relation T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 is O(n) using substitution method.
questions.answer: A recurrence relation defines a function in terms of its value at smaller inputs. Methods: Substitution (guess and verify), Recursion Tree (expand visually), Master Theorem (formula). Substitution for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1: Guess T(n) = O(n). Assume T(n/2) ≤ c(n/2). Then T(n) = 2×c(n/2) + 1 = cn + 1. This is ≤ cn only if 1 ≤ 0, which fails. Subtract lower-order: guess T(n) ≤ cn - 1. T(n) = 2(c(n/2)-1) + 1 = cn - 2 + 1 = cn - 1 ≤ cn - 1. ✓ So T(n) = O(n).

questions.question: Write down the advantages of dynamic programming over greedy strategy. Find optimal bracketing to multiply 4 matrices of order 2, 3, 4, 2, 5.
questions.answer: DP advantages over Greedy: DP considers all possible solutions and picks optimal; greedy makes local choices that may not be globally optimal. DP works for problems without greedy-choice property. DP handles overlapping subproblems. For matrix chain with p=[2,3,4,2,5]: Compute m[i][j] for chain length l=2,3,4. m[1][2]=2×3×4=24, m[2][3]=3×4×2=24, m[3][4]=4×2×5=40. m[1][3]=min(m[1][1]+m[2][3]+2×3×2, m[1][2]+m[3][3]+2×4×2)=min(36,40)=36 at k=1. m[2][4]=min(m[2][2]+m[3][4]+3×4×5, m[2][3]+m[4][4]+3×2×5)=min(100,54)=54 at k=3. m[1][4]=min(m[1][1]+m[2][4]+2×3×5, m[1][2]+m[3][4]+2×4×5, m[1][3]+m[4][4]+2×2×5)=min(138,120,76)=76 at k=3. Optimal parenthesization: ((AB)(CD)) split at k=3, or equivalently (A(BC))D with cost 76.

questions.question: Discuss heapify operation with example. Write down its algorithm and analyze its time and space complexity.
questions.answer: Heapify maintains the max-heap property. MAX-HEAPIFY(A, i): left=2i, right=2i+1. largest = i. If left ≤ heap-size and A[left] > A[largest]: largest=left. If right ≤ heap-size and A[right] > A[largest]: largest=right. If largest ≠ i: swap A[i] and A[largest], recursively MAX-HEAPIFY(A, largest). Example: Array [4, 10, 3, 5, 1] — heapify at root: compare 4 with children 10 and 3; 10 is largest; swap 4 and 10 → [10, 4, 3, 5, 1]; heapify at index 2 (value 4): compare with children 5,1; swap 4 and 5 → [10, 5, 3, 4, 1]. Time: O(log n) since tree height is log n. Space: O(log n) for recursion stack, O(1) iteratively.

questions.question: Define RAM model. Write down iterative algorithm for finding factorial and provide its detailed analysis.
questions.answer: RAM (Random Access Machine) model: Simplified model of computation where each basic operation (arithmetic, comparison, memory access) takes constant time O(1). Memory is unlimited and accessible in O(1). FACTORIAL(n): result=1; for i=1 to n: result = result×i; return result. Analysis: Initialization: 1 step. Loop runs n times: each iteration does 1 multiplication and 1 increment = 2 operations. Total: 1 + 2n operations = O(n). Space: O(1) — only two variables. This is a linear time, constant space algorithm.

questions.question: Write down algorithm of insertion sort and analyze its time and space complexity.
questions.answer: INSERTION-SORT(A): for j=2 to n: key=A[j]; i=j-1; while i>0 and A[i]>key: A[i+1]=A[i]; i=i-1; A[i+1]=key. Best case: Array already sorted; inner while never executes. Comparisons = n-1. Time O(n). Worst case: Reverse sorted; inner while runs j-1 times for each j. Total comparisons = 1+2+...+(n-1) = n(n-1)/2. Time O(n²). Average case: O(n²). Space: O(1) — in-place algorithm. Stable sort.

questions.question: Write down minmax algorithm and analyze its complexity.
questions.answer: MINMAX(A, low, high): Divide and conquer approach. If only 1 element: min=max=A[low]. If 2 elements: compare and return. Else: mid=(low+high)/2; (lmin,lmax)=MINMAX(A,low,mid); (rmin,rmax)=MINMAX(A,mid+1,high); return (min(lmin,rmin), max(lmax,rmax)). Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 2 comparisons. Solution: T(n) = 3n/2 - 2 comparisons (for n=2ᵏ). This is optimal — requires at least 3n/2 - 2 comparisons in worst case. Time O(n), Space O(log n) for recursion.

questions.question: When does greedy strategy provide optimal solution? Write down job sequencing with deadlines algorithm and analyze its complexity.
questions.answer: Greedy gives optimal solution when the problem has: (1) Greedy-choice property — a globally optimal solution can be reached by making locally optimal choices, and (2) Optimal substructure — optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems. Job Sequencing: Sort jobs by decreasing profit. For each job (in sorted order): find latest free time slot before deadline; if found, schedule job there. ALGORITHM: Sort by profit; for each job, find slot d[i] to 1; if slot free, assign job. Time O(n²) for naive slot finding, O(n log n) with union-find. Space O(n).

questions.question: Suppose that a message contains alphabet frequencies as given below and find Huffman codes for each alphabet. Symbols: a, b, c, d, e; Frequencies: 30, 20, 25, 15, 35.
questions.answer: Frequencies: a=30, b=20, c=25, d=15, e=35. Build min-heap: {d:15, b:20, c:25, a:30, e:35}. Step 1: Merge d(15) and b(20) → db(35). Heap: {c:25, a:30, e:35, db:35}. Step 2: Merge c(25) and a(30) → ca(55). Heap: {e:35, db:35, ca:55}. Step 3: Merge e(35) and db(35) → edb(70). Heap: {ca:55, edb:70}. Step 4: Merge ca(55) and edb(70) → root(125). Codes: a=00, c=01, e=10, d=110, b=111. (Note: code assignment depends on left/right choice; any valid prefix code with these lengths is acceptable: a,c,e get 2-bit codes, d,b get 3-bit codes).

questions.question: Does backtracking give multiple solutions? Trace subset sum algorithm for the set {3, 5, 2, 4, 1} and sum = 8.
questions.answer: Yes, backtracking can give multiple solutions for subset sum. Trace for {3,5,2,4,1}, sum=8: Sort: {1,2,3,4,5}. Explore: {1,2,3,4}=10>8 prune; {1,2,5}=8 ✓; {1,3,4}=8 ✓; {1,7} none; {2,3,?}=5, need 3: {2,3,3} none; {2,6} none; {3,5}=8 ✓; {4,?} no single. Also {1,2,3,?}=6, need 2: already used. {1,3,?}=4, need 4: {1,3,4}=8 already counted. Solutions: {1,2,5}, {1,3,4}, {3,5}.

questions.question: Why is extended Euclidean algorithm used? Write down its algorithm and analyze its complexity.
questions.answer: Extended Euclidean Algorithm finds GCD(a,b) AND coefficients x, y such that ax + by = GCD(a,b). Used in: modular inverse (RSA key generation), solving linear Diophantine equations, Chinese Remainder Theorem. EXTENDED-GCD(a,b): if b=0: return (a,1,0); else: (g,x1,y1) = EXTENDED-GCD(b, a mod b); x=y1; y=x1-(a div b)×y1; return (g,x,y). Complexity: Same as Euclidean algorithm — O(log(min(a,b))) recursive calls. Each call reduces the problem by roughly the Fibonacci ratio. Time O(log n), Space O(log n) for recursion stack.

questions.question: Define NP-complete problems with examples. Give brief proof of the statement 'SAT is NP-complete'.
questions.answer: NP-Complete: Problems that are in NP and are NP-Hard (every NP problem reduces to them in polynomial time). Examples: SAT, 3-SAT, Vertex Cover, Clique, Independent Set, Subset Sum, Hamiltonian Cycle, TSP. SAT is NP-Complete (Cook's Theorem 1971): (1) SAT ∈ NP: Given a truth assignment, we can verify it satisfies the formula in polynomial time. (2) SAT is NP-Hard: For any NP problem L, there is a polynomial reduction to SAT. Any NP problem can be computed by a non-deterministic Turing machine M in polynomial time. The computation of M on input x can be encoded as a Boolean formula φ that is satisfiable iff M accepts x. This reduction is polynomial. Therefore SAT is NP-Complete.

questions.question: Write short notes on: (a) Aggregate Analysis.
questions.answer: Aggregate Analysis is an amortized analysis technique that computes the total cost of a sequence of n operations and divides by n to get average cost per operation. Unlike worst-case per-operation analysis, it gives a tighter bound. Example: Dynamic array doubling — individual push can cost O(n) when resizing, but over n pushes, total cost is O(n) (sum of doubling costs: 1+2+4+...+n = 2n). Amortized cost per push = O(n)/n = O(1).

questions.question: Write short notes on: (b) Selection problems.
questions.answer: Selection Problem: Find the i-th smallest element in an unsorted array. Naive: Sort in O(n log n), return element at index i. Expected linear time (Randomized Select): Use quicksort partition; after partitioning, recurse only on the side containing the i-th element. Expected O(n). Worst-case linear time (Median of Medians): Divide into groups of 5, find median of each group, find median of medians as pivot, guaranteed O(n) worst case. Special cases: i=1 (minimum), i=n (maximum) each take O(n) with one pass.

questions.question: Explain the divide and conquer strategy for problem solving. Describe the worst-case linear time selection algorithm and analyze its complexity.
questions.answer: Divide and Conquer: (1) Divide the problem into smaller subproblems. (2) Conquer by solving subproblems recursively. (3) Combine solutions. Examples: Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Binary Search. Worst-case linear time selection (Median of Medians): (1) Divide n elements into groups of 5. (2) Find median of each group. (3) Recursively find median of medians (M). (4) Partition around M. (5) Recurse on appropriate partition. Analysis: T(n) ≤ T(n/5) + T(7n/10 + 6) + O(n). Solves to T(n) = O(n). The key: partition eliminates at least 3n/10 elements.

questions.question: Write the dynamic programming algorithm for matrix chain multiplication. Find the optimal parenthesization for the matrix chain product ABCD with sizes: A=5x10, B=10x15, C=15x20, D=20x30.

What do you mean by Backtracking? Explain the backtracking algorithm for solving 0-1 knapsack problem and find the solution for the problem given below. Items→ 1 2 3 4; Weight(wi)→ 2 3 4 5; Profit(Pi)→ 3 5 6 10; capacity = 10 kg.
questions.answer: Backtracking: A systematic method that tries all possibilities and abandons paths that cannot lead to a solution. It uses DFS with pruning — when a partial solution cannot be extended to a complete valid solution, it backtracks and tries another path. 0-1 Knapsack Backtracking: Sort items by decreasing profit/weight if helpful. Use bounding function. Explore include/exclude for each item. For given data: Item 1 (w2,p3), Item 2 (w3,p5), Item 3 (w4,p6), Item 4 (w5,p10). Capacity=10. Possible valid subsets: {1,2,3,4}=14>10 no; {2,3,4}=12>10 no; {1,3,4}=11>10 no; {1,2,4}=10≤10 profit=18; {1,2,3}=9≤10 profit=14; {2,4}=8≤10 profit=15; {3,4}=9≤10 profit=16; {1,4}=7≤10 profit=13. Maximum profit = 18 with items {1,2,4} (weights 2+3+5=10).

questions.question: Explain the iterative algorithm to find the GCD of given two numbers and analyze its complexity.
questions.answer: Euclidean Algorithm (iterative): GCD(a,b): while b≠0: temp=b; b=a mod b; a=temp; return a. Example: GCD(48,18): 48 mod 18=12, GCD(18,12); 18 mod 12=6, GCD(12,6); 12 mod 6=0, GCD(6,0)=6. Complexity: Each iteration, the smaller number is replaced by the remainder. By Lamé's theorem, the number of iterations ≤ 5 × (number of decimal digits in min(a,b)). Time complexity: O(log(min(a,b))). Space: O(1) iteratively.

questions.question: Generate the prefix code for the string 'CYBER CRIME' using Huffman algorithm and find the total number of bits required.
questions.answer: Count frequencies in 'CYBER CRIME' (11 chars, space=1): C=2, Y=1, B=1, E=2, R=2, I=1, M=1, space=1. Build Huffman tree by repeatedly merging two lowest frequency nodes. Assign 0/1 to branches. Characters with higher frequency get shorter codes. Typical prefix codes: C=00, E=01, R=10, B=1100, I=1101, M=1110, Y=11110, space=11111. Total bits = 2×2 + 2×2 + 2×2 + 1×4 + 1×4 + 1×4 + 1×4 + 1×5 = 4+4+4+4+4+4+4+5 = 33 bits (approximate; exact depends on tree structure, but typically 32-36 bits for this distribution). Compared to 11×8=88 bits for ASCII, compression ratio ≈ 0.38.

questions.question: Define tractable and intractable problems. Illustrate vertex cover problem with an example.
questions.answer: Tractable: Problems solvable in polynomial time O(nᵏ). Examples: sorting (O(n log n)), shortest path (O(n²)). Intractable: Problems with no known polynomial-time algorithm. No efficient solution exists. Examples: TSP, Subset Sum, Hamiltonian Cycle. Vertex Cover: Find the minimum set S of vertices such that every edge has at least one endpoint in S. NP-Complete problem. Example: Graph with vertices {A,B,C,D,E} and edges {(A,B),(B,C),(C,D),(D,E),(E,A),(B,D)}: Minimum vertex cover = {B,D,E} — every edge is incident to at least one of these. Brute force: check all 2ⁿ subsets. For large n, intractable.

questions.question: Find the edit distance between the string 'ARTIFICIAL' and 'NATURAL' using dynamic programming.
questions.answer: Edit Distance between 'ARTIFICIAL' (10 chars) and 'NATURAL' (7 chars) using DP. Build (11×8) table. dp[i][j] = min edits to convert first i chars of ARTIFICIAL to first j chars of NATURAL. Operations: insert, delete, substitute (cost 1). Fill row by row. Characters: A,R,T,I,F,I,C,I,A,L vs N,A,T,U,R,A,L. Result: edit distance = 6 (requires: N→A substitution, A→R substitution, T stays, U→T substitution, R→I substitution, A→F substitution, insert C, insert I, A stays, L stays; or equivalent optimal path). The DP table confirms distance 6.

questions.question: Write short notes on: (a) Best, Worst and average case complexity.
questions.answer: Best Case: Minimum number of operations performed on most favorable input. Example: Sequential search finds element at first position — O(1). Worst Case: Maximum operations on most unfavorable input. Sequential search — element not found or at last position — O(n). Average Case: Expected number of operations over all possible inputs assuming uniform distribution. Sequential search: element equally likely at any position — O(n/2) = O(n). Worst case is most commonly analyzed for algorithm guarantees.

questions.question: Write short notes on: (b) Greedy Strategy.
questions.answer: Greedy Strategy: At each step, make the locally optimal choice hoping it leads to a global optimum. No backtracking. Fast and simple but does not always give optimal solution. Works when: (1) Greedy-choice property holds — local optimal leads to global optimal, and (2) Optimal substructure — optimal solution contains optimal substructure. Examples where greedy works: Huffman coding, Fractional Knapsack, MST (Kruskal, Prim), Dijkstra's. Examples where greedy fails: 0-1 Knapsack, TSP, general coin change.

questions.question: Solve the following recurrence relations using master's method: (a) T(n) = 2T(n/4) + kn²; (b) T(n) = 5T(n/4) + kn.
questions.answer: (a) T(n) = 2T(n/4) + kn²: a=2, b=4, f(n)=kn². log_b(a)=log₄(2)=0.5. f(n)=kn²=Ω(n^(0.5+ε)) — Case 3. Regularity: 2×k(n/4)² = kn²/8 ≤ (1/8)kn² ✓. T(n)=Θ(n²). (b) T(n) = 5T(n/4) + kn: a=5, b=4, f(n)=kn. log₄(5) ≈ 1.16. f(n)=kn=O(n^(1.16-ε))—Case 1. T(n)=Θ(n^log₄(5))=Θ(n^1.16).

questions.question: Solve the following linear congruences using Chinese Remainder Theorem: x ≡ 1 (mod 2), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 6 (mod 7).

Find the MST from the given graph using Kruskal's algorithm. [Graph: Undirected weighted graph with vertices A-G. Edges: A-D(1), B-E(1), C-D(1), D-E(1), A-B(2), A-C(2), C-F(2), E-G(3), B-D(5), D-G(5), D-F(6), F-G(10)]
questions.answer: Kruskal's Algorithm: Sort all edges by weight. Initialize each vertex as its own component. Process edges in order: A-D(1) ✓, B-E(1) ✓, C-D(1) ✓, D-E(1) ✓ (connects components), A-B(2) skip (cycle A-D-E-B), A-C(2) skip (cycle A-D-C), C-F(2) ✓. Now all vertices A,B,C,D,E,F connected. Need G: E-G(3) ✓. Total edges = 6 (for 7 vertices). MST edges: A-D(1), B-E(1), C-D(1), D-E(1), C-F(2), E-G(3). Total weight = 1+1+1+1+2+3 = 9.

questions.question: Trace the quick sort algorithm for sorting the array A[] = {15, 7, 6, 23, 18, 34, 25} and write its best and worst complexity.
questions.answer: Quick Sort on {15,7,6,23,18,34,25}, pivot=last element (25): Partition: elements ≤25 go left, >25 go right. After partition: {15,7,6,23,18,25,34}, pivot 25 at index 5. Recurse on {15,7,6,23,18} with pivot 18: partition → {15,7,6,18,23}. Recurse on {15,7,6} with pivot 6: partition → {6,7,15}. Continue until sorted: {6,7,15,18,23,25,34}. Best case: pivot always divides array into equal halves → T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) → O(n log n). Worst case: pivot is always min or max (sorted array with last as pivot) → T(n)=T(n-1)+O(n) → O(n²).

questions.question: What are the elementary properties of algorithm? Explain. Why do you need algorithm? Discuss about analysis of the RAM model for analysis of algorithm with suitable example.
questions.answer: Elementary properties of algorithm: (1) Input — zero or more externally supplied quantities. (2) Output — at least one quantity is produced. (3) Definiteness — each instruction is clear and unambiguous. (4) Finiteness — algorithm terminates after finite steps. (5) Effectiveness — every instruction is basic enough to be carried out. We need algorithms to solve problems systematically, automate tasks, and ensure correctness and efficiency. RAM model analysis: Each basic operation (arithmetic, comparison, memory access) takes O(1). Example: factorial algorithm takes O(n) time and O(1) space under RAM model.

questions.question: Explain about the divide and conquer paradigm for algorithm design with suitable example. Write the Quick sort algorithm using randomized approach and explain its time complexity.
questions.answer: Divide and Conquer: (1) Divide problem into subproblems. (2) Conquer subproblems recursively. (3) Combine solutions. Example: Merge Sort — divide array into halves, sort each half, merge. Randomized Quick Sort: RANDOMIZED-QUICKSORT(A,p,r): if p<r, q=RANDOMIZED-PARTITION(A,p,r), recurse on both sides. RANDOMIZED-PARTITION selects random pivot, swaps with last element, then standard partition. Time: Best/Average O(n log n), Worst O(n²) but extremely unlikely due to randomization. Expected O(n log n).

questions.question: Explain in brief about the Dynamic Programming Approach for algorithm design. How does it differ from recursion? Explain the algorithm for solving the 0/1 Knapsack problem using the dynamic programming approach and explain its complexity.
questions.answer: Dynamic Programming: Solves problems by breaking into overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem once, and storing results. Key elements: optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. DP vs Recursion: Recursion may recompute subproblems exponentially; DP stores results (bottom-up or memoization) to avoid recomputation. 0/1 Knapsack DP: dp[i][w] = max value using first i items with capacity w. dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w-wi]+vi) if wi≤w, else dp[i-1][w]. Fill table for n items and capacity W. Time O(nW), Space O(nW) or optimized O(W).

questions.question: Explain the recursion tree method for solving recurrence relations. Solve the following recurrence relation using this method: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 for n > 1, T(1) = 1 for n = 1.
questions.answer: Recursion Tree: Visualize recursive calls as a tree. At each node, write the non-recursive cost. Sum costs across all levels. T(n)=2T(n/2)+1: Level 0: cost 1. Level 1: 2 nodes, each cost 1 → total 2. Level 2: 4 nodes, each cost 1 → total 4. ... Level i: 2ⁱ nodes, total cost 2ⁱ. Tree height: log₂n. Total cost = 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n = 2n - 1 = O(n). Therefore T(n) = Θ(n).

questions.question: Write an algorithm to find the maximum element of an array and analyze its time complexity.
questions.answer: MAX-ELEMENT(A): max = A[1]; for i=2 to n: if A[i] > max: max = A[i]; return max. Time: O(n) — single pass through n elements, n-1 comparisons. Space: O(1) — only one variable. This is optimal as any algorithm must examine all n elements in the worst case.

questions.question: Write the algorithm for bubble sort and explain its time complexity.
questions.answer: BUBBLE-SORT(A): for i=1 to n-1: for j=1 to n-i: if A[j] > A[j+1]: swap A[j] and A[j+1]. Best case (sorted): O(n) with optimization flag. Worst case (reverse sorted): O(n²) — n(n-1)/2 comparisons and swaps. Average case: O(n²). Space: O(1). Stable sort. Simple but inefficient for large datasets.

questions.question: What do you mean by optimization problem? Explain the greedy strategy for algorithm design to solve optimization problems.
questions.answer: Optimization Problem: Find the best solution (maximum or minimum) from all feasible solutions according to an objective function. Examples: shortest path, minimum spanning tree, maximum profit. Greedy Strategy: (1) At each step, make the locally optimal choice. (2) Never reconsider choices (no backtracking). (3) Hope local choices lead to global optimum. Requires: Greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. Examples: Fractional Knapsack, Huffman coding, MST algorithms.

questions.question: Explain the algorithm and its complexity for solving job sequencing with deadline problem using greedy strategy.
questions.answer: Job Sequencing with Deadlines: Given n jobs with deadlines and profits, schedule maximum profit jobs before deadlines. Greedy approach: Sort jobs by decreasing profit. For each job, find the latest available slot before its deadline. If slot exists, schedule job there. Algorithm: Sort by profit O(n log n). For each job, scan slots from deadline down to 1 O(n). Total O(n²). With union-find for slot finding: O(n log n). Space O(n). Guarantees maximum profit because greedy-choice holds: highest profit job should be scheduled if possible.

questions.question: What do you mean by memorization strategy? Compare memorization with dynamic programming.
questions.answer: Memoization: Top-down dynamic programming. Use recursion but store results of computed subproblems in a table (memo). Before computing, check if result exists. If yes, return stored value. Memoization vs DP: (1) Memoization is top-down (recursion + cache); DP is bottom-up (iterative table filling). (2) Memoization computes only needed subproblems; DP computes all subproblems. (3) Memoization has recursive overhead; DP has no recursion overhead. (4) Both have same time complexity for same subproblems. (5) DP often has better constant factors and space optimization.

questions.question: Explain the concept of backtracking. How does it differ from recursion?
questions.answer: Backtracking: Systematic trial-and-error method that builds candidates incrementally and abandons partial candidates ('backtracks') as soon as they cannot lead to a valid solution. Uses DFS with pruning. Recursion vs Backtracking: Recursion is a general technique where a function calls itself. Backtracking uses recursion but adds the ability to undo choices and explore alternatives. All backtracking uses recursion, but not all recursion is backtracking. Backtracking is used for constraint satisfaction (N-Queen, subset sum); recursion is used for divide-and-conquer, tree traversal, etc.

questions.question: Explain in brief about the complexity classes P, NP, and NP-Complete.
questions.answer: Class P: Decision problems solvable by deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time. Examples: sorting, shortest path, primality testing. Class NP: Decision problems where a proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time. P ⊆ NP. NP-Complete: The hardest problems in NP. A problem is NP-Complete if: (1) it is in NP, and (2) every NP problem can be reduced to it in polynomial time. Examples: SAT, 3-SAT, Vertex Cover, Clique, Hamiltonian Cycle, TSP (decision version). If any NP-Complete problem has a polynomial-time algorithm, then P = NP.

questions.question: Write short notes on: (a) NP Hard Problems and NP Completeness.
questions.answer: NP-Hard: Problems at least as hard as the hardest problems in NP. A problem X is NP-Hard if every NP problem can be reduced to X in polynomial time. X need not be in NP. Examples: Halting Problem, TSP (optimization version), Chess. NP-Completeness: A problem is NP-Complete if it is both in NP and NP-Hard. To prove NP-Completeness: (1) Show problem ∈ NP, (2) Show a known NP-Complete problem reduces to it. SAT was the first NP-Complete problem (Cook's Theorem).

questions.question: Write short notes on: (b) Problem Reduction.
questions.answer: Problem Reduction: Transforming instances of problem A into instances of problem B such that solving B solves A. Polynomial reduction (A ≤ₚ B): transformation takes polynomial time. Used to prove NP-Completeness and compare problem difficulty. If A ≤ₚ B and B is easy, then A is easy. If A ≤ₚ B and A is hard, then B is hard. Examples: SAT ≤ₚ 3-SAT, 3-SAT ≤ₚ Vertex Cover, Vertex Cover ≤ₚ Subset Sum.

questions.question: Write down the elements of dynamic programming. Give the recursive definition of LCS problem. Find LCS between sequences S1='Dinesh', S2='Dikshya'.
questions.answer: Elements of DP: (1) Optimal substructure — optimal solution contains optimal subsolutions. (2) Overlapping subproblems — same subproblems solved repeatedly. (3) Memoization or tabulation to store results. LCS recursive definition: LCS(i,j) = 0 if i=0 or j=0; LCS(i,j) = 1 + LCS(i-1,j-1) if X[i]=Y[j]; else LCS(i,j) = max(LCS(i-1,j), LCS(i,j-1)). For 'Dinesh' and 'Dikshya': D-i-n-e-s-h vs D-i-k-s-h-y-a. LCS = 'Dish' (length 4). DP table confirms: D(1), i(2), n/k skip, e/s skip, s(3), h(4).

questions.question: What is heap? Sort the following data items by using heap sort: A[] = {3, 5, 2, 66, 4, 11, 9, 34}.
questions.answer: Heap: Complete binary tree satisfying heap property — max-heap: parent ≥ children; min-heap: parent ≤ children. Heap Sort: (1) Build max-heap from array. (2) Repeatedly extract maximum (swap root with last element, reduce heap size, heapify root). For A={3,5,2,66,4,11,9,34}: Build max-heap → {66,34,11,5,4,2,9,3}. Extract 66 → swap with 3, heapify → {34,5,11,3,4,2,9}. Extract 34 → swap with 9, heapify → {11,5,9,3,4,2}. Extract 11 → swap with 2, heapify → {9,5,2,3,4}. Continue: {9,5,4,3,2} → {5,4,2,3} → {4,3,2} → {3,2} → {2}. Sorted: {2,3,4,5,9,11,34,66}. Time O(n log n), Space O(1) in-place.

questions.question: Given a set S = {6, 4, 5, 6, 9} and X = 11. Obtain the subset sum using backtracking approach.
questions.answer: Sort: {4,5,6,6,9}. Use backtracking with pruning. Explore: {4,5}=9, need 2 (none). {4,6}=10, need 1 (none). {4,6}=10 (second 6), need 1 (none). {4,9}=13>11 prune. {5,6}=11 ✓. {5,6}=11 (second 6) ✓. {6,?}=6, need 5: {6,5}=11 already counted. {6,9}=15>11 prune. {9,?}=9, need 2 (none). Valid subsets: {5,6} using either of the two 6s. If elements are distinct positions: {4,5,?} no; {5,6}=11; {6,?} no other. Solutions: {5,6} (two possible if both 6s are distinct items).

questions.question: Write down algorithm of insertion sort and analyze its time and space complexity.
questions.answer: INSERTION-SORT(A): for j=2 to n: key=A[j]; i=j-1; while i>0 and A[i]>key: A[i+1]=A[i]; i=i-1; A[i+1]=key. Best case (sorted): O(n) — n-1 comparisons, no shifts. Worst case (reverse sorted): O(n²) — total shifts = n(n-1)/2. Average case: O(n²). Space: O(1) in-place. Stable sort. Efficient for small or nearly sorted arrays.

questions.question: Define binary search algorithm. Write down the recursive algorithm for binary search and analyze it.
questions.answer: Binary Search: Find element x in sorted array A. Compare x with middle element. If equal, found. If x < middle, search left half. If x > middle, search right half. Recursive algorithm: BINARY-SEARCH(A, low, high, x): if low > high return NOT_FOUND; mid = (low+high)/2; if A[mid]==x return mid; if x < A[mid] return BINARY-SEARCH(A, low, mid-1, x); else return BINARY-SEARCH(A, mid+1, high, x). Time: O(log n) — halves search space each step. Space: O(log n) recursion stack, O(1) iterative.

questions.question: Explain the asymptotic notations used to describe the time/space complexity of any algorithm.
questions.answer: Asymptotic Notations: Big-O (O): Upper bound. f(n)=O(g(n)) if ∃c,n₀: f(n)≤c·g(n) ∀n≥n₀. Describes worst-case. Big-Ω (Omega): Lower bound. f(n)=Ω(g(n)) if ∃c,n₀: f(n)≥c·g(n) ∀n≥n₀. Describes best-case. Big-Θ (Theta): Tight bound. f(n)=Θ(g(n)) if f(n)=O(g(n)) and f(n)=Ω(g(n)). Describes exact growth. Little-o: Strict upper bound. Little-ω: Strict lower bound. These notations ignore constant factors and lower-order terms, focusing on growth rate as n→∞.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Euclid's algorithm? Explain with suitable example.
questions.answer: Euclid's Algorithm finds the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) of two integers. It is one of the oldest algorithms still in use. Based on the principle that GCD(a,b) = GCD(b, a mod b). Example: GCD(48,18): 48 = 2×18 + 12; GCD(18,12): 18 = 1×12 + 6; GCD(12,6): 12 = 2×6 + 0. GCD = 6. Time: O(log(min(a,b))). Space: O(1). Extended version also finds coefficients x,y such that ax+by=GCD(a,b), used in RSA for modular inverses.

questions.question: Solve the recurrence relation T(n) = T(n-1) + 1 when T(0) = 0.
questions.answer: T(n) = T(n-1) + 1, T(0)=0. Expand: T(n) = T(n-1)+1 = [T(n-2)+1]+1 = T(n-2)+2 = ... = T(0)+n = 0+n = n. Therefore T(n) = O(n). This is a linear recurrence representing a simple loop that does constant work n times. Verification: T(1)=T(0)+1=1, T(2)=T(1)+1=2, T(3)=3 — pattern holds.

questions.question: Define greedy algorithm. Find minimum spanning tree of the following graph by using Kruskal algorithm. [Graph: Undirected weighted graph with vertices 1-6. Edges: 1-4(1), 1-2(2), 2-4(3), 2-3(3), 1-5(4), 3-4(5), 2-6(7), 3-6(8), 4-5(9)]
questions.answer: Greedy Algorithm: Makes locally optimal choice at each step with hope of global optimum. Requires greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. Kruskal's on given graph: Sort edges by weight: 1-4(1), 1-2(2), 2-4(3), 2-3(3), 1-5(4), 3-4(5), 2-6(7), 3-6(8), 4-5(9). Process: 1-4(1) ✓, 1-2(2) ✓, 2-4(3) skip (cycle 1-2-4), 2-3(3) ✓, 1-5(4) ✓, 3-4(5) skip (cycle), 2-6(7) ✓. All 6 vertices connected with 5 edges. MST edges: 1-4(1), 1-2(2), 2-3(3), 1-5(4), 2-6(7). Total weight = 1+2+3+4+7 = 17.

questions.question: Explain in brief about the classes P, NP, and NP-Complete with examples.
questions.answer: Class P: Decision problems solvable in polynomial time by deterministic Turing machine. Examples: sorting, shortest path, GCD, primality testing. Class NP: Decision problems verifiable in polynomial time. Examples: SAT, Hamiltonian Cycle (verification easy, finding hard). P ⊆ NP. NP-Complete: Hardest in NP — in NP and every NP problem reduces to it. Examples: SAT, 3-SAT, Vertex Cover, Clique, Subset Sum. If P=NP, all NP-Complete problems have polynomial solutions. Currently believed P≠NP.

questions.question: Find the optimal parenthesization for the matrix chain product ABCD with sizes: A = 5x10, B = 10x15, C = 15x20, D = 20x30.
Write short notes on: (a) Best, Worst and average case complexity.
questions.answer: Best Case: Minimum operations on most favorable input. Example: element found at first position in search — O(1). Worst Case: Maximum operations on most unfavorable input. Example: element not found or at last position — O(n). Average Case: Expected operations over all inputs with uniform distribution. Example: average position in search is n/2 — O(n). Worst-case analysis provides performance guarantees; average-case gives realistic expectations; best-case is rarely useful alone.

questions.question: Write short notes on: (b) Backtracking strategy.
questions.answer: Backtracking Strategy: (1) Define solution space. (2) Organize as tree (state space tree). (3) Use DFS to explore. (4) At each node, check constraints. (5) If constraints violated, backtrack to parent and try next branch. (6) If leaf reached with valid solution, record it. Applications: N-Queen, subset sum, graph coloring, Hamiltonian cycle, maze solving. Pruning (bounding) improves efficiency by skipping unpromising branches.

questions.question: Differentiate between greedy and dynamic programming. Solve the 0-1 Knapsack problem for items with weights [2,3,4,5] and values [3,4,5,6] with capacity W=5 using DP.
questions.answer: Greedy makes locally optimal choices without reconsideration; may not give global optimum. DP explores all subproblems and guarantees global optimum through optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. 0-1 Knapsack DP: Build table dp[i][w] for i items and capacity w. dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], dp[i-1][w-wi]+vi) if wi≤w, else dp[i-1][w]. Fill table: dp[1][2]=3, dp[1][3..5]=3; dp[2][3]=4, dp[2][5]=max(3,4+3)=7; dp[3][4]=5, dp[3][5]=max(7,5)=7; dp[4][5]=max(7,6)=7. Maximum value = 7 (items 1 and 2: weight 2+3=5, value 3+4=7).

questions.question: Explain recursion tree method with example. Solve T(n) = 3T(n/3) + n using recursion tree.
questions.answer: Recursion Tree: Draw the recursion as a tree. At each node, show the work done at that level excluding recursive calls. Sum the costs across all levels. T(n) = 3T(n/3) + n: Level 0: n. Level 1: 3 nodes, each n/3 work → n total. Level 2: 9 nodes, each n/9 → n total. Tree height: log₃(n). Total levels: log₃(n) + 1. Total cost: n × (log₃(n) + 1) = O(n log n).

questions.question: What is backtracking? Solve the N-Queen problem for N=4 using backtracking.
questions.answer: Backtracking: Builds solution incrementally, abandons partial solutions that fail constraints (backtracks). N-Queen (N=4): Place 4 queens on 4×4 board with no two attacking each other. Try row 1: Q at col 1. Row 2: col 1 attacked, col 2 diagonal, try col 3. Row 3: col 1,3 attacked; try col 1 diagonal, col 2 ok? Q1 at (1,1), Q2 at (2,3), Q3 must avoid cols 1,3,2,4. No valid position → backtrack. Q2 at (2,4), Q3 at (3,2), Q4 at (4,?) → col 4 and col 1 safe? (4,4) attacks (3,3), try (4,1): attacks (3,2) diag. No solution with Q1 at col 1. Try Q1 at col 2: Solution: {(1,2),(2,4),(3,1),(4,3)}.

questions.question: Prove that n² + 3n + 1 = O(n²) using the definition of Big-O notation.
questions.answer: By definition, f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist constants c>0 and n₀≥1 such that f(n) ≤ c×g(n) for all n≥n₀. We need: n²+3n+1 ≤ c×n² for all n≥n₀. Divide by n²: 1 + 3/n + 1/n² ≤ c. For n≥1: 3/n ≤ 3 and 1/n² ≤ 1. So: 1+3/n+1/n² ≤ 1+3+1=5. Choose c=5, n₀=1. Then n²+3n+1 ≤ 5n² for all n≥1. Therefore n²+3n+1 = O(n²). ∎

questions.question: Explain the purpose of Huffman coding. Build a Huffman tree for characters with frequencies: A=45, B=13, C=12, D=16, E=9, F=5.
questions.answer: Huffman Coding: Variable-length prefix code for data compression. More frequent characters get shorter codes. No code is a prefix of another. Build min-heap: F:5, E:9, C:12, B:13, D:16, A:45. Merge F(5)+E(9)=FE(14). Heap: C:12, B:13, FE:14, D:16, A:45. Merge C(12)+B(13)=CB(25). Heap: FE:14, D:16, CB:25, A:45. Merge FE(14)+D(16)=FED(30). Heap: CB:25, FED:30, A:45. Merge CB(25)+FED(30)=CBFED(55). Heap: A:45, CBFED:55. Merge→root(100). Codes: A=0 (1 bit), CBFED left subtree: CB left: C=100, B=101; FED right: F=1100, E=1101, D=111. Avg length=(45×1+13×3+12×3+16×3+9×4+5×4)/100=2.24 bits vs 3 for fixed.

questions.question: Apply Extended Euclidean Algorithm to find GCD(252, 198) and express it as a linear combination.
Explain the concept of NP-completeness and describe how to prove a problem is NP-complete.
questions.answer: NP-Completeness: A problem X is NP-Complete if (1) X ∈ NP — solutions can be verified in polynomial time, and (2) X is NP-Hard — every NP problem can be reduced to X in polynomial time. To prove X is NP-Complete: Step 1: Show X ∈ NP — describe a polynomial-time verifier for X. Step 2: Choose a known NP-Complete problem Y. Step 3: Show Y ≤ₚ X — construct a polynomial-time reduction from Y to X (transform any Y instance to X instance such that Y is satisfiable iff X is satisfiable). Conclusion: Since Y is NP-Complete and Y reduces to X, and X ∈ NP, X is NP-Complete.

questions.question: Apply Floyd-Warshall algorithm on a graph with vertices A, B, C and edges A→B (weight 3), B→C (weight 2), A→C (weight 10), C→A (weight 1).
Describe the average case analysis of Quick Sort.
questions.answer: Average case analysis of Quick Sort assumes all permutations of the input are equally likely. Let T(n) be the expected number of comparisons. After choosing pivot, suppose it ends at position k (1 ≤ k ≤ n), creating partitions of size k-1 and n-k. T(n) = (n-1) + (1/n) × Σ(k=1 to n)[T(k-1) + T(n-k)]. By symmetry: T(n) = (n-1) + (2/n) × Σ(k=0 to n-1)[T(k)]. Solving: T(n) = O(n log n). Specifically, T(n) ≈ 1.39 n log₂n comparisons — about 39% worse than merge sort but usually faster in practice due to cache effects and small constant.

questions.question: Compare Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms for finding MST.
questions.answer: Kruskal's: Edge-based. Sort all edges by weight. Add edge if it doesn't form cycle (use union-find). Works well for sparse graphs. Time O(E log E) or O(E log V). Prim's: Vertex-based. Start from any vertex, greedily add minimum weight edge connecting tree to non-tree vertex. Works well for dense graphs. Time O(V²) with adjacency matrix, O(E log V) with binary heap. Both produce correct MST. Kruskal's is simpler to implement for sparse graphs. Prim's is better for dense graphs. Both are greedy algorithms with optimal substructure guaranteed.

questions.question: State and prove Fermat's little theorem. How is it used in primality testing?
questions.answer: Fermat's Little Theorem: If p is prime and a is not divisible by p, then a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Proof sketch: Consider {a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p-1)a} mod p — these are all distinct and non-zero, hence a permutation of {1,2,...,p-1}. Product: a^(p-1) × (p-1)! ≡ (p-1)! (mod p). Divide by (p-1)! (valid since gcd((p-1)!,p)=1): a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Primality Testing (Fermat Test): Choose random a; compute a^(n-1) mod n; if ≠1, n is composite. Limitation: Carmichael numbers pass for all a but are composite. Miller-Rabin fixes this with additional squaring steps.

questions.question: Explain memoization with an example. Compute the 6th Fibonacci number using memoization.
questions.answer: Memoization: Top-down DP — store results of already-solved subproblems in a memo table (dictionary/array). Before computing, check if result already exists. Avoids redundant recomputation. FIB-MEMO(n, memo): if n in memo: return memo[n]; if n≤1: return n; memo[n] = FIB-MEMO(n-1,memo) + FIB-MEMO(n-2,memo); return memo[n]. Computing FIB(6): FIB(6)→FIB(5)+FIB(4). FIB(5)→FIB(4)+FIB(3). FIB(4)→FIB(3)+FIB(2). FIB(3)→FIB(2)+FIB(1)=1+1=2. FIB(2)=1. FIB(4)=2+1=3. FIB(3)=2 (cached). FIB(5)=3+2=5. FIB(4)=3 (cached). FIB(6)=5+3=8. Each subproblem computed once. Time O(n), Space O(n).

Section B (5-mark, attempt 8 of 9) reliably covers Recurrence/Master Theorem, Asymptotic notation, Backtracking/Subset Sum, Extended Euclidean, CRT, Miller-Rabin, NP/Cook's Theorem, Vertex Cover approximation, and Edit Distance. Edit Distance (String Editing) has appeared 3 out of 4 years — nearly guaranteed. Backtracking appears every year. DP appears every year in Section A. Huffman appears 3 of 4 years. Prim's/Dijkstra have never appeared directly — possible wildcard.
